newsitem.title: USA: Thai sovereign credit unhurt by bank woes - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Thai sovereign credit unhurt by bank woes - S&P.

text.p: The problems that currently plague the Thai banking system are manageable and will not affect Thailand's long-term sovereign ratings, said the U.S. credit rating agency, Standard and Poor's.
At a teleconference on Thursday, S&P sovereign analysts said the government credit should be distinguished from private banking credit.
Thailand currently has single A for its long-term foreign currency debt and double A for its long-term local currency debt. The outlook remains stable, the analysts said.
The downturn of the property market and the general slowdown of the economy brought problems to rising non- performing loans to Thai financial companies and banks, said the S&P analyst from Melbourn.
While the problems exist mainly among the financing companies, commercial banks are expected to come under pressure in the next one to three years, he said.

The Thai central bank has taken initiative to encourage merger of weak financial companies with each other or with banks, but "the positive measures may not be sufficient to contain the problems within the property sector," he said.

Specifically, declining value of the collaterals and increasing bad loan provision requirements would keep profitability on the capital level under pressure, the analyst said. But since the medium-term profitability outlook for the banks remains "satisfactory" in the medium term, that would give banks time to solve the growing problem of asset quality, he added.
From the perspective of sovereign credit, "the magnitude of the problem is manageable," said S&P's sovereign analyst, Cem Karacadag, in New York.

"The key fundamental credit strength and weakness of Thailand has not unchanged, which is why we maintain the stable outlook for the single A on foreign currency and double A on local currency rating on the kingdom," he said.
With its long-standing conservative monetary policy, high savings rate, an open economic system and flexible labor market, Thailand's economic structure is sound, he noted.

Karacadag acknowledged that bailing out failed banks by the government could affect the sovereign creditworthiness, but he asserted that the Thai government has the resources to cope with the potential losses.

In the worst scenario, the bad loans would not exceed six percent of the Gross Domestic Product, and the government has the ability to "withstand even a higher degree of losses," he said, noting: "Thailand has a proven track record of adjusting to shocks in the past."
Karacadag expected that the Bank of Thailand would adhere to the current exchange rate policy, which is a "de-facto" fixed rate regime.
To keep a stable currency, the central bank has to keep the interest rates high, which in turn would put pressure on the private sector, especially the banks, he said.
